claim: A new opsin sequence from Leptochiton asellus possesses the Pfam tm7_1 domain.
source: The sequence possesses the Pfam tm7_1 domain, Lys296 (referring to homologous bovine opsin positions), which is predictive for opsin chromophore binding, as well as the NPXXY motif and the tripeptide motif on positon 310–312 crucial for G-protein activation (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript states that the sequence possesses specific domains and motifs characteristic of opsins, based on domain and motif analyses.

claim: The new L. asellus opsin sequence contains Lys296, which is predictive for opsin chromophore binding.
source: The sequence possesses the Pfam tm7_1 domain, Lys296 (referring to homologous bovine opsin positions), which is predictive for opsin chromophore binding, as well as the NPXXY motif and the tripeptide motif on positon 310–312 crucial for G-protein activation (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript identifies Lys296 in the sequence and states its predictive role for chromophore binding, drawing on established knowledge of opsin structure.

claim: The new L. asellus opsin sequence contains the NPXXY motif.
source: The sequence possesses the Pfam tm7_1 domain, Lys296 (referring to homologous bovine opsin positions), which is predictive for opsin chromophore binding, as well as the NPXXY motif and the tripeptide motif on positon 310–312 crucial for G-protein activation (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports the presence of the NPXXY motif based on sequence analysis.

claim: The new L. asellus opsin sequence contains a tripeptide motif at position 310-312 crucial for G-protein activation.
source: The sequence possesses the Pfam tm7_1 domain, Lys296 (referring to homologous bovine opsin positions), which is predictive for opsin chromophore binding, as well as the NPXXY motif and the tripeptide motif on positon 310–312 crucial for G-protein activation (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript identifies a tripeptide motif at specific positions and states its role in G-protein activation based on established knowledge.

claim: The tripeptide motif in the new L. asellus opsin matches the NKQ motif characteristic for c-opsins.
source: The latter matches the NKQ motif, which is characteristic for c-opsins but is also present in some sequences of the recently described group of xenopsins (Ramirez et al., 2016) and a few cnidops.
evidence: The manuscript states that the tripeptide motif matches NKQ and cites Ramirez et al., 2016 for the presence of this motif in xenopsins.

claim: The NKQ motif is also present in some xenopsin sequences.
source: The latter matches the NKQ motif, which is characteristic for c-opsins but is also present in some sequences of the recently described group of xenopsins (Ramirez et al., 2016) and a few cnidops.
evidence: The manuscript cites Ramirez et al., 2016 to support the presence of NKQ motif in xenopsins.

claim: Several sequences initially described as c-opsins fall into xenopsins according to Ramirez et al. (2016).
source: Correct placement of the new L. asellus opsin is highly relevant for our study and, according to Ramirez et al. (2016), several sequences initially described as c-opsins fall into xenopsins.
evidence: The manuscript cites Ramirez et al., 2016 for the reclassification of certain sequences from c-opsins to xenopsins.

claim: Maximum-likelihood and Bayesian analyses yielded nearly identical tree topologies for opsin phylogeny.
source: Subsequent maximum-likelihood and Bayesian runs yielded nearly identical tree topologies.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of phylogenetic analyses showing congruence between different methods.

claim: C-opsins and xenopsins form distinct and highly supported groups in phylogenetic analysis.
source: In line with the study by Ramirez et al. (2016), c-opsins and xenopsins form distinct and highly supported groups (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports phylogenetic results and references figures showing the distinct grouping, consistent with Ramirez et al., 2016.

claim: The new opsin from L. asellus groups with high support within xenopsins.
source: The new opsin from L. asellus groups with high support within xenopsins and is thus termed L. asellus xenopsin.
evidence: The manuscript reports the phylogenetic placement of the new opsin based on tree inference results.

claim: Xenopsins were discovered in Owenia fusiformis, a member of the basally branching annelid group of Oweniidae.
source: In addition to the xenopsins reported by Ramirez et al. (2016) from mollusks, brachiopods and rotifers, we discovered this opsin type in Owenia fusiformis, a member of the basally branching annelid group of Oweniidae, in several polyclad flatworms and in the triclad flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea.
evidence: The manuscript reports the discovery of xenopsins in Owenia fusiformis based on transcriptome analysis.

claim: Xenopsins were discovered in several polyclad flatworms.
source: In addition to the xenopsins reported by Ramirez et al. (2016) from mollusks, brachiopods and rotifers, we discovered this opsin type in Owenia fusiformis, a member of the basally branching annelid group of Oweniidae, in several polyclad flatworms and in the triclad flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea.
evidence: The manuscript reports the discovery of xenopsins in polyclad flatworms based on transcriptome analysis.

claim: Xenopsins were discovered in the triclad flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea.
source: In addition to the xenopsins reported by Ramirez et al. (2016) from mollusks, brachiopods and rotifers, we discovered this opsin type in Owenia fusiformis, a member of the basally branching annelid group of Oweniidae, in several polyclad flatworms and in the triclad flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea.
evidence: The manuscript reports the discovery of xenopsins in Schmidtea mediterranea based on database screening.

claim: No c-opsin or xenopsin was found in nine screened RNA-seq datasets from acoelomorphs or xenoturbellids.
source: We did not find any c-opsin or xenopsin in the nine screened RNA-seq datasets from acoelomorphs or xenoturbellids.
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of c-opsins and xenopsins in screened datasets.

claim: No hints of c-opsins or xenopsins were found in any nemertean species from nine screened RNA-seq datasets.
source: From the nine screened RNA-seq datasets, we found higher numbers of opsin sequences only in Lineus longissimus, but no hints that there are c-opsins or xenopsins in any nemertean species.
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of c-opsins and xenopsins in nemertean datasets.

claim: Xenopsin paralogs of several platyhelminth species are distributed across two well-supported xenopsin subgroups.
source: Further, our data suggest that xenopsins diversified at an early stage of protostome evolution. Xenopsin paralogs of several platyhelminth species are distributed across two well-supported xenopsin subgroups, one of which also contains sequences from many other protostome taxa (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports phylogenetic results showing the distribution of platyhelminth xenopsins across subgroups.

claim: Xenopsins diversified at an early stage of protostome evolution.
source: Further, our data suggest that xenopsins diversified at an early stage of protostome evolution.
evidence: The manuscript infers early diversification based on the phylogenetic distribution of xenopsins across protostome taxa.

claim: Three introns are highly conserved in position and phase throughout protostome c-opsins, deuterostome encephalopsins, TMT opsins, VA-opsins, parapinopsins and pinopsins, and vertebrate visual opsins.
source: Three introns are highly conserved in position and phase (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) throughout protostome c-opsins, deuterostome encephalopsins, TMT opsins, VA-opsins, parapinopsins and pinopsins, and the vertebrate visual opsins.
evidence: The manuscript reports gene structure analysis showing conserved intron positions across multiple opsin groups.

claim: All xenopsins share two different intron positions with conserved intron phase, with the exception of one sequence from Adineta vaga.
source: By contrast, all xenopsins share two different intron positions with conserved intron phase (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3), with the exception of one sequence from Adineta vaga.
evidence: The manuscript reports gene structure analysis showing conserved intron positions in xenopsins.

claim: The three conserved c-opsin and two xenopsin introns do not overlap in position.
source: The xenopsin and c-opsin intron positions do not overlap in any of the alignments.
evidence: The manuscript reports that gene structure analysis across multiple alignments shows no overlap between c-opsin and xenopsin intron positions.

claim: Gene structure provides strong evidence that xenopsins and c-opsins are distinct opsin subgroups.
source: Thus, gene structure provides strong evidence that xenopsins and c-opsins are indeed distinct opsin subgroups, irrespective of their mutually exclusive distribution amongst bilaterian animals.
evidence: The manuscript concludes that gene structure data support the phylogenetic distinction between xenopsins and c-opsins.

claim: Las-xenopsin is expressed in the posttrochal eye region of L. asellus larvae.
source: This revealed expression in the posttrochal eye region (Figures 1B and 3F) as well as in cells at the very apical (Figure 1B inset) and posterior ends of the larva (Figure 1C), an expression pattern strongly resembling that of Las-ropsin (Vöcking et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results showing Las-xenopsin expression in the eye region.

claim: Las-xenopsin is expressed in cells at the apical end of L. asellus larvae.
source: This revealed expression in the posttrochal eye region (Figures 1B and 3F) as well as in cells at the very apical (Figure 1B inset) and posterior ends of the larva (Figure 1C), an expression pattern strongly resembling that of Las-ropsin (Vöcking et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results showing Las-xenopsin expression at the apical end.

claim: Las-xenopsin is expressed in cells at the posterior end of L. asellus larvae.
source: This revealed expression in the posttrochal eye region (Figures 1B and 3F) as well as in cells at the very apical (Figure 1B inset) and posterior ends of the larva (Figure 1C), an expression pattern strongly resembling that of Las-ropsin (Vöcking et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results showing Las-xenopsin expression at the posterior end.

claim: Las-xenopsin and Las-r-opsin are co-expressed in all eye photoreceptor cells of L. asellus.
source: Double in-situ hybridization unambiguously showed cellular coexpression of Las-xenopsin and Las-ropsin in all PRCs (Figures 3F and 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports double in situ hybridization results showing co-expression of both opsins in photoreceptor cells.

claim: Eye photoreceptor cells of L. asellus have microvillar-like vertical extensions.
source: (b) Microvillar-like vertical extensions of the eye PRC.
evidence: The manuscript describes electron microscopy observations of microvillar structures in photoreceptor cells.

claim: Two cilia emerge from each eye photoreceptor cell in L. asellus.
source: Indeed, we found two cilia in each PRC in addition to the many microvillar extensions (Figure 3A,C,D), corroborating ultrastructural data from other chitons (Bartolomaeus, 1992; Fischer, 1980; Rosen et al., 1979).
evidence: The manuscript reports electron microscopy observations and cites previous ultrastructural studies in chitons.

claim: The cilia in L. asellus eye photoreceptor cells show a 9 × 2 + 2 microtubule pattern.
source: The cilia show a 9 × 2 + 2 microtubule pattern (Figure 3C inset).
evidence: The manuscript reports electron microscopy observations of ciliary structure.

claim: The cilia in L. asellus eye photoreceptor cells do not exceed the cuticle.
source: Neither the cilia nor the microvillae exceed the cuticle nor exhibit specialized surface extensions (Figure 3A,C), but they are longer than the rudimentary cilia found in surrounding epithelial cells and do not taper (Figure 3A,C,E).
evidence: The manuscript reports electron microscopy observations of ciliary structure relative to the cuticle.

claim: Las-Foxj1 is expressed in the photoreceptor cells of 7 dpf L. asellus larvae.
source: Both are expressed in the PRCs of 7 dpf L. asellus larvae (Figure 4G,H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and Las-Foxj1 was also found to be expressed in the prototroch cells and the apical organ of younger larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results showing Las-Foxj1 expression in photoreceptor cells.

claim: Las-RFX is expressed in the photoreceptor cells of 7 dpf L. asellus larvae.
source: Both are expressed in the PRCs of 7 dpf L. asellus larvae (Figure 4G,H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and Las-Foxj1 was also found to be expressed in the prototroch cells and the apical organ of younger larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results showing Las-RFX expression in photoreceptor cells.

claim: Las-Arf4 is specifically expressed in the photoreceptor cells of L. asellus.
source: Several ortholgos of the general players of ciliary targeting that are also active in ciliary opsin targeting, namely Las-Arf4, Las-rab8, Las-FIP3, Las-RPGR and Las-MyosinVIIa (Liu et al., 1999; Wang and Deretic, 2014, 2015; Wang et al., 2012), were found to be specifically expressed in the PRCs by double in-situ hybridization with Las-r-opsin (Figure 4B–F, Figure 4—figure supplements 3–5).
evidence: The manuscript reports double in situ hybridization results showing Las-Arf4 expression in photoreceptor cells and cites studies on ciliary opsin targeting.

claim: Las-rab8 is specifically expressed in the photoreceptor cells of L. asellus.
source: Several ortholgos of the general players of ciliary targeting that are also active in ciliary opsin targeting, namely Las-Arf4, Las-rab8, Las-FIP3, Las-RPGR and Las-MyosinVIIa (Liu et al., 1999; Wang and Deretic, 2014, 2015; Wang et al., 2012), were found to be specifically expressed in the PRCs by double in-situ hybridization with Las-r-opsin (Figure 4B–F, Figure 4—figure supplements 3–5).
evidence: The manuscript reports double in situ hybridization results showing Las-rab8 expression in photoreceptor cells and cites studies on ciliary opsin targeting.

claim: Las-FIP3 is specifically expressed in the photoreceptor cells of L. asellus.
source: Several ortholgos of the general players of ciliary targeting that are also active in ciliary opsin targeting, namely Las-Arf4, Las-rab8, Las-FIP3, Las-RPGR and Las-MyosinVIIa (Liu et al., 1999; Wang and Deretic, 2014, 2015; Wang et al., 2012), were found to be specifically expressed in the PRCs by double in-situ hybridization with Las-r-opsin (Figure 4B–F, Figure 4—figure supplements 3–5).
evidence: The manuscript reports double in situ hybridization results showing Las-FIP3 expression in photoreceptor cells and cites studies on ciliary opsin targeting.

claim: Las-RPGR is specifically expressed in the photoreceptor cells of L. asellus.
source: Several ortholgos of the general players of ciliary targeting that are also active in ciliary opsin targeting, namely Las-Arf4, Las-rab8, Las-FIP3, Las-RPGR and Las-MyosinVIIa (Liu et al., 1999; Wang and Deretic, 2014, 2015; Wang et al., 2012), were found to be specifically expressed in the PRCs by double in-situ hybridization with Las-r-opsin (Figure 4B–F, Figure 4—figure supplements 3–5).
evidence: The manuscript reports double in situ hybridization results showing Las-RPGR expression in photoreceptor cells and cites studies on ciliary opsin targeting.

claim: Las-MyosinVIIa is specifically expressed in the photoreceptor cells of L. asellus.
source: Several ortholgos of the general players of ciliary targeting that are also active in ciliary opsin targeting, namely Las-Arf4, Las-rab8, Las-FIP3, Las-RPGR and Las-MyosinVIIa (Liu et al., 1999; Wang and Deretic, 2014, 2015; Wang et al., 2012), were found to be specifically expressed in the PRCs by double in-situ hybridization with Las-r-opsin (Figure 4B–F, Figure 4—figure supplements 3–5).
evidence: The manuscript reports double in situ hybridization results showing Las-MyosinVIIa expression in photoreceptor cells and cites studies on ciliary opsin targeting.

claim: The C-terminal VxPx motif necessary for Arf4-mediated transport of vertebrate c-opsins is missing in xenopsins.
source: As the C-terminal VxPx motif necessary for the Arf4-mediated transport of vertebrate c-opsins (Wang and Deretic, 2014) is missing in xenopsins, Arf4-mediated transport of xenopsin would require other protein interactions.
evidence: The manuscript reports sequence analysis showing the absence of the VxPx motif in xenopsins and cites Wang and Deretic, 2014 for the role of this motif in vertebrate c-opsin transport.

claim: The VxPx motif is only conserved in tunicate and vertebrate c-opsins, but not in cephalochordate, echinoderm and protostome c-opsins, xenopsins, cnidops or any other opsin-type.
source: Interestingly, the same holds true for ciliary transport of cnidops and of c-opsins from organisms other than vertebrates and tunicates, as the VxPx motif is only conserved in the latter opsin groups and not in cephalochordate, echinoderm or protostome c-opsins or cnidops, some of which have been shown to be expressed in ciliary PRCs (Arendt et al., 2004; Bielecki et al., 2014; Kozmik et al., 2008; Vopalensky et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript reports sequence analysis showing the restricted conservation of the VxPx motif and cites studies on ciliary PRC expression.

claim: No species possessing both c-opsins and xenopsins was found despite screening genomic resources for many species.
source: Even though genomic resources were screened for many species, stunningly we could not recover a single species possessing both c-opsins and xenopsins.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of extensive database screening showing mutually exclusive distribution of c-opsins and xenopsins.

claim: C-opsins and xenopsins show mutually exclusive distribution at higher taxonomic levels in deuterostomes and major protostome clades.
source: This also holds true for higher taxonomic levels, since as sequences of just one of the two opsin groups were found in deuterostomes and in major protostome clades such as mollusks, rotifers, brachiopods, flatworms, arthropods and tardigrades.
evidence: The manuscript reports the taxonomic distribution of c-opsins and xenopsins based on database screening.

claim: Xenopsins but no c-opsins were found in the annelid Owenia fusiformis.
source: As the only exception, we found xenopsins (but no c-opsins) in the annelid Owenia fusiformis, whereas other annelids such as Platynereis dumerilii possess only c-opsins or lack both types as do Capitella teleta or Helobdella robusta (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the presence of xenopsins and absence of c-opsins in Owenia fusiformis based on transcriptome analysis.

claim: Platynereis dumerilii possesses only c-opsins.
source: As the only exception, we found xenopsins (but no c-opsins) in the annelid Owenia fusiformis, whereas other annelids such as Platynereis dumerilii possess only c-opsins or lack both types as do Capitella teleta or Helobdella robusta (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the presence of c-opsins in Platynereis dumerilii based on sequence data.

claim: Capitella teleta lacks both c-opsins and xenopsins.
source: As the only exception, we found xenopsins (but no c-opsins) in the annelid Owenia fusiformis, whereas other annelids such as Platynereis dumerilii possess only c-opsins or lack both types as do Capitella teleta or Helobdella robusta (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of both c-opsins and xenopsins in Capitella teleta based on sequence data.

claim: Helobdella robusta lacks both c-opsins and xenopsins.
source: As the only exception, we found xenopsins (but no c-opsins) in the annelid Owenia fusiformis, whereas other annelids such as Platynereis dumerilii possess only c-opsins or lack both types as do Capitella teleta or Helobdella robusta (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of both c-opsins and xenopsins in Helobdella robusta based on sequence data.

claim: Xenopsins are present in mollusks, rotifers, brachiopods, flatworms, and Oweniidae annelids.
source: Our data reveal a broader occurrence of xenopsins in protostomes than hitherto anticipated, pointing towards a high relevance of this opsin type in animal physiology. Accordingly, xenopsins are present not only in mollusks, rotifers and brachiopods as already reported by Ramirez et al. (2016), but also in several flatworms and in Oweniidae, the first branch within annelids.
evidence: The manuscript reports the taxonomic distribution of xenopsins based on database screening and transcriptome analysis.

claim: There is no evidence that xenopsins exist in deuterostomes.
source: In accordance with Ramirez et al. (2016), we have no evidence that xenopsins exist in deuterostomes.
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of xenopsins in deuterostomes based on database screening, consistent with Ramirez et al., 2016.

claim: Xenopsins were already present in the last common ancestor of deuterostomes and protostomes.
source: Nevertheless, the data provide clear evidence that xenopsins were already present in the last common ancestor of deuterostomes and protostomes.
evidence: The manuscript infers the ancestral presence of xenopsins based on their phylogenetic distribution across bilaterian animals.

claim: Xenopsins form the sister group to cnidops in phylogenetic analysis.
source: In the analysis of Ramirez et al. (2016) and in our study, xenopsins form the sister group to cnidops, and this may very likely reflect the evolutionary history.
evidence: The manuscript reports phylogenetic results showing the sister group relationship between xenopsins and cnidops, consistent with Ramirez et al., 2016.

claim: Frequent lineage-specific loss of either xenopsins or c-opsins during animal evolution has to be assumed.
source: According to our data, frequent lineage-specific loss of either xenopsins or c-opsins (or both) during animal evolution has to be assumed.
evidence: The manuscript infers frequent gene loss based on the mutually exclusive distribution of c-opsins and xenopsins across taxa.

claim: The NKQ tripeptide motif present in L. asellus xenopsin is known to be involved in GNAI- and cGMP-based signaling of c-opsins.
source: By contrast, the NKQ tripeptide motif present in L. asellus xenopsin is known to be involved in the GNAI- and cGMP-based signaling (Marin et al., 2000) of c-opsins and is similar to motifs in cnidops, some of which were shown to mediate GNAS- and cAMP-based signaling (Koyanagi et al., 2008; Liegertová et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites Marin et al., 2000 for the role of the NKQ motif in c-opsin signaling.

claim: The NKQ motif in L. asellus xenopsin is similar to motifs in cnidops that mediate GNAS- and cAMP-based signaling.
source: By contrast, the NKQ tripeptide motif present in L. asellus xenopsin is known to be involved in the GNAI- and cGMP-based signaling (Marin et al., 2000) of c-opsins and is similar to motifs in cnidops, some of which were shown to mediate GNAS- and cAMP-based signaling (Koyanagi et al., 2008; Liegertová et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites Koyanagi et al., 2008 and Liegertová et al., 2015 for the signaling properties of cnidops.

claim: The L. asellus eye photoreceptor cells express all relevant elements of standard r-opsin-mediated GNAQ-dependent IP3 signaling.
source: The L. asellus eye PRCs express all relevant elements of standard r-opsin-mediated GNAQ-dependent IP3 signaling (Vöcking et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites Vöcking et al., 2015 for the expression of r-opsin signaling components in L. asellus photoreceptor cells.

claim: Xenopsin is employed in the purely ciliary photoreceptor cells of the larval eyes of the brachiopod Terebratalia transversa.
source: Xenopsins are seemingly able to enter cilia. This type of opsin is employed in the purely ciliary PRCs of the larval eyes of the brachiopod Terebratalia transversa (Passamaneck et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites Passamaneck et al., 2011 for the expression of xenopsin in ciliary photoreceptor cells of brachiopod larval eyes.

claim: All existing data on the expression of xenopsins point towards their presence in eyes.
source: By contrast, all existing data on the expression of xenopsins point towards their presence in eyes.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes expression data from multiple sources showing xenopsin presence in eyes.

claim: RNA-seq data from cephalopods suggest the presence of xenopsins in eyes.
source: RNA-seq data from cephalopods likewise suggest the presence of xenopsins in eyes (Yoshida et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites Yoshida et al., 2015 for RNA-seq data suggesting xenopsin presence in cephalopod eyes.

claim: Photoreceptor cells in insects enlarge the sensory area by microvilli and depolarize in response to light.
source: The PRCs in insects have been shown to enlarge the sensory area by microvilli and to depolarize in response to light, whereas vertebrate eyes are hyperpolarizing and bear a modified cilium (Eakin, 1963; 1968, 1979).
evidence: The manuscript cites Eakin, 1963; 1968, 1979 for the structural and electrophysiological properties of insect photoreceptor cells.

claim: Vertebrate eye photoreceptor cells are hyperpolarizing and bear a modified cilium.
source: The PRCs in insects have been shown to enlarge the sensory area by microvilli and to depolarize in response to light, whereas vertebrate eyes are hyperpolarizing and bear a modified cilium (Eakin, 1963; 1968, 1979).
evidence: The manuscript cites Eakin, 1963; 1968, 1979 for the structural and electrophysiological properties of vertebrate photoreceptor cells.

claim: Two conserved photoreceptor cell types are the main sensory components of animal cerebral eyes: microvillar depolarizing r-opsin-expressing PRCs and ciliary hyperpolarizing c-opsin-expressing cells.
source: Subsequent data on molecular physiology and transcriptional regulation of cell specification allowed much more detailed characterization of PRCs,suggesting that two conserved PRC types are indeed the main sensory components of animal cerebral eyes: (a) microvillar depolarizing r-opsin-expressing PRCs, which signal via the Gq-mediated IP3 cascade, and (b) ciliary hyperpolarizing c-opsin-expressing cells, which signal via the Gi/t-mediated cGMP cascade (Arendt et al., 2002a, 2004; Fain et al., 2010; Fernald, 2006; Gehring, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies (Arendt et al., 2002a, 2004; Fain et al., 2010; Fernald, 2006; Gehring, 2014) for the classification of photoreceptor cell types based on molecular physiology.

claim: Microvillar r-opsin-expressing photoreceptor cells signal via the Gq-mediated IP3 cascade.
source: Subsequent data on molecular physiology and transcriptional regulation of cell specification allowed much more detailed characterization of PRCs,suggesting that two conserved PRC types are indeed the main sensory components of animal cerebral eyes: (a) microvillar depolarizing r-opsin-expressing PRCs, which signal via the Gq-mediated IP3 cascade, and (b) ciliary hyperpolarizing c-opsin-expressing cells, which signal via the Gi/t-mediated cGMP cascade (Arendt et al., 2002a, 2004; Fain et al., 2010; Fernald, 2006; Gehring, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies for the signaling mechanism of r-opsin-expressing photoreceptor cells.

claim: Ciliary c-opsin-expressing photoreceptor cells signal via the Gi/t-mediated cGMP cascade.
source: Subsequent data on molecular physiology and transcriptional regulation of cell specification allowed much more detailed characterization of PRCs,suggesting that two conserved PRC types are indeed the main sensory components of animal cerebral eyes: (a) microvillar depolarizing r-opsin-expressing PRCs, which signal via the Gq-mediated IP3 cascade, and (b) ciliary hyperpolarizing c-opsin-expressing cells, which signal via the Gi/t-mediated cGMP cascade (Arendt et al., 2002a, 2004; Fain et al., 2010; Fernald, 2006; Gehring, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies for the signaling mechanism of c-opsin-expressing photoreceptor cells.

claim: R-opsin+ photoreceptor cells are present in the ganglion cell layer of vertebrate eyes, where they are involved in the pupillary reflex and the entrainment of the circadian clock.
source: The r-opsin+ type of PRCs constitutes the main visual elements in many protostome cerebral eyes, but they are also present in the ganglion cell layer of vertebrate eyes, where they are involved in the pupillary reflex and the entrainment of the circadian clock (Hattar et al., 2003; Koyanagi et al., 2005; Panda et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites Hattar et al., 2003; Koyanagi et al., 2005; Panda et al., 2002 for the presence and function of r-opsin+ cells in vertebrate eyes.

claim: C-opsins were initially reported only in arthropod and annelid deep brain photoreceptors.
source: In protostomes, c-opsins were initially reported only in arthropod and annelid deep brain photoreceptors (Arendt et al., 2004; Velarde et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites Arendt et al., 2004 and Velarde et al., 2005 for the initial reports of c-opsins in protostome brain photoreceptors.

claim: It was assumed that c-opsin was ancestrally employed by unpigmented brain photoreceptor cells fulfilling non-visual functions and were only secondarily integrated into the eyes of chordates.
source: It was assumed, therefore, that this visual pigment was ancestrally employed by unpigmented brain PRCs that were fulfilling non-visual functions and were only secondarily integrated into the eyes of chordates (Arendt et al., 2004; Vopalensky et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites Arendt et al., 2004 and Vopalensky et al., 2012 for the hypothesis about the ancestral function of c-opsins.

claim: Reports on the presence of ciliary photoreceptor cells and c-opsins in the eyes of protostomes challenged the view that c-opsins were ancestrally employed only in brain photoreceptors.
source: Reports on the presence of ciliary PRCs and c-opsins in the eyes of protostomes challenged this view and also the concept of gradually evolving ancient PRC types in animal eyes.
evidence: The manuscript discusses how new findings challenged previous hypotheses about c-opsin evolution.

claim: A flexible employment of different opsin types by eye photoreceptor cells or frequent gain and loss of photoreceptor cell types in cerebral eyes during the evolution of bilaterian animals were suggested.
source: Accordingly, a rather flexible employment of different opsin types by eye photoreceptor cells or frequent gain and loss of photoreceptor cell types in cerebral eyes during the evolution of bilaterian animals were suggested (Passamaneck et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites Passamaneck et al., 2011 for the hypothesis of flexible opsin employment in eye evolution.

claim: Several protostome sequences initially classified as c-opsins fall into the xenopsin group.
source: Advances in opsin phylogeny, however, suggest that several protostome sequences, which share characteristic sequence motifs with c-opsins and were initially classified as such, fall into their own group, now termed xenopsins (Ramirez et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Ramirez et al., 2016 for the reclassification of certain sequences from c-opsins to xenopsins.

claim: DS-GTR+Γ is the best fitting model for opsin phylogenetic analysis according to Akaike information, Bayesian information and Decision theory criteria.
source: In ProtTest 3.4, the implemented model FLU was exchanged against our DS-GTR, revealing DS-GTR+Γ as best fitting model according to Akaike information, Bayesian information and Decision theory criteria (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports model selection results showing DS-GTR+Γ as the best fitting model.

claim: DS-GTR CAT and GTR CAT are the best non-parametric variants for Bayesian opsin phylogenetic analysis.
source: As a result, DS-GTR CAT and GTR CAT were found to be the best non-parametric variants, performing better than the best parametric variant DS-GTR Γ, and all three of these were better than any empirical mixture modeling (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript reports cross-validation results comparing different models for Bayesian analysis.

claim: The vast majority of photoreceptor cells express only one type of visual opsin.
source: As a general observation, the vast majority of PRCs express only one type of visual opsin.
evidence: The manuscript states a general observation about opsin expression in photoreceptor cells based on existing knowledge.

claim: In nearly all cases where more than one visual opsin was found in photoreceptor cells, the respective opsins belong to the same opsin subgroup and evoke the same phototransduction cascade.
source: In nearly all cases where more than one visual opsin was found in PRCs, the respective opsins belong to the same opsin subgroup and evoke the same phototransduction cascade.
evidence: The manuscript states a general pattern about co-expression of opsins in photoreceptor cells based on existing knowledge.

claim: Co-expression of r-opsins has been shown in the eye photoreceptor cells of Limulus polyphemus.
source: This has been shown for r-opsins in several arthropods, as for example in the eye PRCs of Limulus polyphemus (Katti et al., 2010), fiddler crabs (Rajkumar et al., 2010) and a butterfly (Arikawa et al., 2003), and for c-opsins in for example mice (Applebury et al., 2000), guinea pigs (Parry and Bowmaker, 2016), salamander (Isayama et al., 2014) and cichlid fishes (Dalton et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites Katti et al., 2010 for co-expression of r-opsins in Limulus polyphemus.

claim: Co-expression of c-opsins has been shown in mice.
source: This has been shown for r-opsins in several arthropods, as for example in the eye PRCs of Limulus polyphemus (Katti et al., 2010), fiddler crabs (Rajkumar et al., 2010) and a butterfly (Arikawa et al., 2003), and for c-opsins in for example mice (Applebury et al., 2000), guinea pigs (Parry and Bowmaker, 2016), salamander (Isayama et al., 2014) and cichlid fishes (Dalton et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites Applebury et al., 2000 for co-expression of c-opsins in mice.

claim: In most cases of opsin co-expression, expansion or tuning of the visual spectrum is the suggested function.
source: In most cases, expansion or tuning of the visual spectrum is the suggested function.
evidence: The manuscript states a general interpretation of the function of opsin co-expression based on existing knowledge.

claim: Go-opsins and r-opsin are co-expressed in eye photoreceptor cells of the annelid Platynereis dumerilii.
source: Co-expression of opsins belonging to different, evolutionary distinct opsin types is reported only very rarely, as in the case of the annelid P. dumerilii, where Go-opsins and r-opsin are employed in eye PRCs (Gühmann et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites Gühmann et al., 2015 for co-expression of Go-opsins and r-opsin in Platynereis dumerilii.

claim: In Platynereis dumerilii, the main function of co-expressing Go-opsins and r-opsin seems to be the expansion of the visual spectrum of the cells.
source: Here, the main function likewise seems to be the expansion of the visual spectrum of the cells.
evidence: The manuscript infers the function of opsin co-expression in Platynereis dumerilii based on the cited study.

claim: Co-expressed opsins evoke competing signaling cascades in the pineal of the lizard Uta stasburiana.
source: To our knowledge, the only case known in which co-expressed opsins evoke competing signaling cascades is in the pineal of the lizard Uta stasburiana (Su et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites Su et al., 2006 for the case of competing signaling cascades from co-expressed opsins.

claim: The opsin reported from brachiopod larval eyes by Passamaneck et al. (2011) is a xenopsin.
source: The opsin reported from brachiopod larval eyes (Passamaneck et al., 2011) is a xenopsin.
evidence: The manuscript reclassifies the opsin from Passamaneck et al., 2011 as a xenopsin based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: All c-opsins previously reported from the visual cells of protostome eyes turned out to be xenopsins instead of c-opsins.
source: These data conflicts are resolved by the fact that all c-opsins that were previously reported from the visual cells of protostome eyes turned out to be xenopsins instead of c-opsins, according to Ramirez et al. (2016) and our study .
evidence: The manuscript concludes that previously reported protostome eye c-opsins are xenopsins based on phylogenetic analysis and Ramirez et al., 2016.

claim: A PCR-based report of a true c-opsin in an onychophoran eye is contradicted by cellular expression analysis showing c-opsin is absent from the eye retina layer.
source: The only exception relies on a PCR-based report of a true c-opsin in an onychophoran eye (Eriksson et al., 2013), but this is contradicted by a cellular expression analysis by Beckmann et al. (2015) showing that c-opsin is absent from the eye retina layer and only present deeply within the brain and the optical ganglia.
evidence: The manuscript cites Eriksson et al., 2013 and Beckmann et al., 2015 to show conflicting reports about c-opsin presence in onychophoran eyes.

claim: Cerebral eye photoreceptor cells of mixed microvillar/ciliary organization have been described in some organisms.
source: The cerebral eye PRCs of mixed microvillar/ciliary organization described in some organisms (Blumer, 1996; Hughes, 1970; Zhukov et al., 2006) may have barely maintained the ancestral organization, whereas microvillar eye PRCs may have emerged by reducing the cilia in taxa in which xenopsin was secondarily lost and the only visual pigment that survived is that associated with microvilli.
evidence: The manuscript cites Blumer, 1996; Hughes, 1970; Zhukov et al., 2006 for the description of photoreceptor cells with mixed microvillar/ciliary organization.

claim: Purely ciliary eye photoreceptor cells have been described in several protostomes.
source: Vice versa, purely ciliary eye PRCs, as have been described in several protostomes (Blumer, 1994, 1999; Passamaneck et al., 2011; Woollacott and Eakin, 1973; Zimmer and Woollacott, 1993), may have formed coincidently with downregulation or complete loss of r-opsins.
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies (Blumer, 1994, 1999; Passamaneck et al., 2011; Woollacott and Eakin, 1973; Zimmer and Woollacott, 1993) for the description of purely ciliary photoreceptor cells in protostomes.

claim: Vestigial ciliary structures in invertebrate microvillar eye photoreceptor cells vary in the length and structural organization of the microtubular axoneme and the ciliary rootlet.
source: The vestigial ciliary structures described vary in the length and in the structural organization of the microtubular axonem and the ciliary rootlet, and often only basal bodies are found (Eakin and Westfall, 1964; Eakin, 1972; Turbeville, 1991; Verger-Bocquet, 1992).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies for the description of vestigial ciliary structures in microvillar photoreceptor cells.

claim: Vestigial ciliary structures in microvillar photoreceptor cells were often interpreted as remnants of the motile cilia of the epidermal cells from which the photoreceptor cells initially originated.
source: These structures were often interpreted as remnants of the motile cilia of the epidermal cells from which the PRCs initially originated (Arendt et al., 2009; Eakin 1979, 1982; Mayer, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites Arendt et al., 2009; Eakin 1979, 1982; Mayer, 2006 for the interpretation of vestigial cilia as remnants of motile cilia.

claim: Primary cilia in most kinds of vertebrate cells are considered to be sensory organelles important for proper cell function, intercellular signalling and development.
source: It is worth noting that the often inconspicuous primary cilia known from most kinds of vertebrate cells are considered to be sensory organelles that are important for proper cell function, intercellular signalling and development (Malicki and Johnson, 2017; Singla, 2006; Walz, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites Malicki and Johnson, 2017; Singla, 2006; Walz, 2017 for the sensory function of primary cilia in vertebrate cells.

claim: More and more motile cilia that also display sensory capabilities are being reported.
source: Last but not least, the distinction between motile and sensory cilia is no longer regarded as clear cut. More and more motile cilia that also display sensory capabilities are being reported (Kleene and Van Houten, 2014; Shah et al., 2009; Warner et al., 2014) and the distribution across eukaryotes of molecular components relevant for locomotion and sensation suggests that cilia were enrolled in both functions upon their emergence (Bloodgood, 2010; Johnson and Leroux, 2010; Mitchell, 2007, 2017; Quarmby and Leroux, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies for the dual sensory and motile functions of cilia.

claim: The distribution across eukaryotes of molecular components relevant for locomotion and sensation suggests that cilia were enrolled in both functions upon their emergence.
source: More and more motile cilia that also display sensory capabilities are being reported (Kleene and Van Houten, 2014; Shah et al., 2009; Warner et al., 2014) and the distribution across eukaryotes of molecular components relevant for locomotion and sensation suggests that cilia were enrolled in both functions upon their emergence (Bloodgood, 2010; Johnson and Leroux, 2010; Mitchell, 2007, 2017; Quarmby and Leroux, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies to support the hypothesis that cilia had both locomotory and sensory functions from their evolutionary origin.
